\note{We need to check whether the various types and values defined in this section are still correct.}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{LiteralExpr} &::=& \texttt{(} \texttt{)}\\
&$|$& \emph{NumericLiteralExpr}\\
&$|$& \emph{CharLiteralExpr}\\
&$|$& \emph{StringLiteralExpr}\\
\end{Grammar}

Fortress provides boolean literals, \TYP{()} literal, character literals,
string literals, and numeric literals.  Literals are values; they do not
require evaluation.

\note{From here, copied from F1.0$\beta$.}

The literal \VAR{false} has type
\EXP{\TYP{BooleanLiteral}\llbracket\VAR{false}\rrbracket}.
The literal \VAR{true} has type
\EXP{\TYP{BooleanLiteral}\llbracket\VAR{true}\rrbracket}.
\note{And these are the only values of those types.}

The literal \EXP{()} is the only value with type \TYP{()}.
Whether any given occurrence of \TYP{()} refers to the value \EXP{()} or
to the type \TYP{()} is determined by context.

A character literal has type \TYP{Character}.
Each character literal consists of an abstract character in
\unicode~\cite{Unicode},
enclosed in single quotation marks (for example, `\txt{a}', `\txt{A}',
`\txt{\$}', `\txt{$\alpha$}', `\txt{$\oplus$}').
\marginnote{This is not true: Character literals include ``\b'' and
``LATIN CAPITAL A'', which do not ``consist of'' an abstract character enclosed in
single quotation marks.  I think it's better to remove most of this discussion and
direct the reader to the relevant section of Lexical Structure.
This section should be about {\bf semantics} of literals:
their values and types.}
The single quotes may be either true typographical ``curly'' single quotation marks
or a pair of ordinary apostrophe characters (for example, \txt{'a'}, \txt{'A'}, \txt{'\$'}, \txt{'$\alpha$'}, \txt{'$\oplus$'}).
See \secref{preprocessing-character-literals} for a description of how names of
characters may be used rather than actual characters within character literals,
for example `\txt{APOSTROPHE}' and `\txt{GREEK\_CAPITAL\_LETTER\_GAMMA}'.

A string literal has type \TYP{String}.
Each string literal is a sequence of \unicode\ characters enclosed in double
quotation marks (for example,
``\txt{Hello, world!}'' or ``\txt{$\pi\thinspace r^2$}'').
\marginnote{Again, I think this paragraph should mostly be eliminated and replaced with a pointer to the relevant section of Lexical Structure.

Here's a sentence I wrote as a replacement:
``A string literal (i.e., a sequence of characters enclosed in double quotation marks---see Section 5.10 for details) has type String.''}
The double quotes may be either true typographical ``curly'' double  quotation marks
or a pair of ``neutral'' double-quote characters (for example,
\txt{"Hello, world!"} or \txt{"$\pi\thinspace r^2$"}).
\secref{preprocessing-string-literals} also describes how names of
characters may be used rather than actual characters within string literals.
One may also use the escape sequences \txt{{\char'134}b} and \txt{{\char'134}t}
and \txt{{\char'134}n} and \txt{{\char'134}f} and \txt{{\char'134}r} as described in \cite{JLS}.


\note{We may want to eliminate the distinction between simple and compound numerals,
and just distinguish them by whether they have a radix point or not, when necessary
(i.e., ``Numerals may have a radix point.'').  Again,
that distinction is primarily a syntactic one, and can be discussed there if appropriate.}
Numeric literals in Fortress are referred to as \emph{numerals},
corresponding to various expressible numbers.
Numerals may be either \emph{simple} or \emph{compound}
(as described in \secref{numerals}).

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of digits)
has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is the value of the numeral
interpreted in radix ten.  If the numeral has no leading zeros, or is
the literal \EXP{0}, then it also has type \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}.
\note{Can the type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}
have any value other than what you get from evaluating the corresponding literal?

What is the relationship between \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}
and \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}?

We need to describe the \TYP{Numeral} type hierarchy.
All the numeric/numeral types should be defined and their relations to each other given.
And a reference to where that is done should be appear in this section (probably at the beginning of the section).
}

\note{Ought we discuss digit-group separators here?
Or is that just part of lexical structure?
(I think we intend that a numeral consisting of digits and digit-group separators has
type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n} and \VAR{v}.)}

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of
digits) then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$ be the
radix) has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket}
where $v$ is
the value of the $n$-digit numeral interpreted in radix $r$.

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
the radix point) has type
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is
the value of the numeral, with the radix point deleted,
interpreted in radix ten.

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
the radix point), then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$
be the radix) has the following type:
\begin{Fortress}
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
\end{Fortress}
where $v$ is the value of the $n$-digit numeral, with the radix point
deleted, interpreted in radix $r$.

Every numeral also has type
\EXP{\TYP{Numeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n}, \VAR{m}, \VAR{r}, and \VAR{v}.


Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types
because, as in common mathematical usage,
we expect them to be polymorphic.
For example, consider the numeral \EXP{3.1415926535897932384};
converting it immediately to a floating-point number
may lose precision.
If that numeral is used in an expression
involving floating-point intervals,
it would be better to convert it directly to an interval.
Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
in Fortress).
\Library\ define coercions
from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
and rational numbers (for compound numerals).


\marginnote{What is an ``integer'' in this context?}
In Fortress, dividing two integers using the $/$ operator produces
a \emph{rational number};\marginnote{Not if the second integer is 0.}
this is true regardless of whether
the integers are of type $\mathbb{Z}$ (or \txt{ZZ}),
$\mathbb{Z}64$ (or \txt{ZZ64}), $\mathbb{N}32$ (or \txt{NN32}), or
whatever.  Addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of rationals
are always exact; thus values such as \EXP{1/3} are represented exactly in
Fortress.

\note{We should give an example with a radix specifier.}
Numerals containing a radix point are actually rational
literals; thus \EXP{3.125} has the rational value \EXP{3125/1000}.
The quotient of two integer literals is a static expression
(described in \secref{static-expr}) whose value is rational.
Similarly, a sequence of digits with a radix point followed by the symbol
$\times$ and an integer literal raised to an integer literal,
such as \EXP{6.0221415 \times 10^{23}}
is a static expression whose value is rational.
If such static expressions are mentioned as part of a floating-point
computation, the compiler performs the rational arithmetic exactly and then
converts the result to a floating-point value, thus incurring
at most one floating-point rounding error.
But in general rational computations may also be performed at run time,
not just at compile time.
\note{This specifies too much about the implementation:
I don't think we should mention a compiler at all, except perhaps as informal discussion.
In particular, wouldn't it be correct if this arithmetic were actually deferred and
performed exactly at run time?}


A rational number can be thought of as a pair of integers $p$ and $q$
that have been reduced to ``standard form in lowest terms'';
that is, $q > 0$ and there is no nonzero integer $k$
such that $p \over k$ and $q \over k$ are integers
and $\left| {p \over k} \right| + \left| {q \over k} \right|
	< \left| p \right| + \left| q \right|$.
The type $\mathbb{Q}$ includes all such rational numbers.

The type $\mathbb{Q}^*$ relaxes the requirement $q>0$ to $q \geq 0$ and
includes two extra values, \EXP{1/0} and \EXP{-1/0} (sometimes called ``the
infinite rational'' and ``the indefinite rational'').
\marginnote{Is there any subtyping or coercion relationship between \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}*}?
If \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}*}
then static checking would normally disallow the assignment,
so is this a relaxation to that rule?  If so, the static checker needs to know about it.}
If a value of type $\mathbb{Q}^*$ is assigned to a
variable of type $\mathbb{Q}$, a \TYP{DivisionByZero} is thrown
at run time if the value is \EXP{1/0} or \EXP{-1/0}.

\section{A Numeral Whose Conversions Tie}
\seclabel{numeral-default}

A numeral has a type of its own, from which \library\ define coercions to the
number types (\secref{literals}).
Where the types to which a numeral can be converted are incomparable under
$\morespecificeq$, as \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} are, each
taking a numeral and neither converting into the other, the numeral is read as
a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its
value does not fit in the narrower type.
This holds in either step: in the choice among declarations that are applicable
to the call only with coercion and that the numeral would otherwise leave tied,
and in the instantiation of a type parameter that only numerals fix.
So of the declarations \EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{N}32)} and
\EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32)}, the call \EXP{g(0)} invokes the second; and a
type parameter that only numerals fix, whose bounds \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} satisfy and the numeral's own type does not, is
instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} when \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} holds the numerals'
values.

The rule settles only a tie that a numeral makes.
Where an argument that is not a numeral leaves the declarations applicable to a
call only with coercion tied, no declaration is the most specific, and the call
is a static error.

content.content:
\note{Properties are not yet supported. Of value objects, only strict
equivalence is supported: the interpreter and the compiled code compare two
value objects of one type field by field (\secref{equivalence}).}

\emph{Objects} are values that have \objecttypes\ described in
\secref{object-traits}.
Objects contain \emph{methods} (described in \secref{methods}) and
\emph{fields} (described in \secref{fields}).

An object is a \emph{value object}, a \emph{reference object},
or a \emph{function object}:
It is a function object if it has an arrow type,
a reference object if it has an object trait type
that is not declared with the \KWD{value} modifier
(see \secref{value-objects}),
and a value object otherwise
(i.e., if it has a tuple type, the type (),
or an object trait type declared
with the \KWD{value} modifier).

A value object cannot have mutable fields,
and it is completely determined by its type,
environment and its fields:
Value objects with the same type, environment and fields
are indistinguishable.
Thus, an implementation may freely copy value objects.
Most objects with simple standard types,
such as booleans,
numeric literals,
IEEE floating-point numbers,
integers of every precision,
and rational numbers are value objects.
%
In contrast,
reference objects are thought to ``reside in memory'',
and are identified by an \emph{object reference}.
A new object reference is created
whenever a reference object is constructed,
so that reference objects constructed separately are always distinct.
What about reference objects that have no mutable fields?
Reference objects include
strings
and aggregates such as arrays, lists and sets.
\revision{revival-object-kinds}{The Working Draft of February 2011 named
arbitrary-precision numbers among the reference objects and gave strings no
kind.
The revival decided on 6~November 2026 that the values of the
arbitrary-precision integer and rational types are value objects, as \library\
declare them, and on 6 and 7~November 2026 that strings are reference objects:
two strings are strictly equivalent only when they are one object, and their
text equality is their \EXP{=}.}
%
Function objects are immutable and have no fields.  Identity is not
well-defined for function objects, and attempting to check whether two
functions are equivalent returns an approximate result.
\secref{equivalence} describes object equivalence in further detail.

\subsection{Which objects are value objects}
\seclabel{revival-object-kinds}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] The opening section of \chapref{objects}, its list of
the kinds of objects.
\item[Change] Its sentence on the value objects named booleans, numeric
literals, IEEE floating-point numbers and integers; it now names integers of
every precision and rational numbers too.
Its sentence on the reference objects named arbitrary-precision numbers and
aggregates such as arrays, lists and sets; it now names strings and the
aggregates.
The passage gains one box.
The rule of strict equivalence (\secref{equivalence}) is unchanged: values of
different types are never strictly equivalent, value objects of one type are
when their fields are, a binary word by its bit pattern, and reference objects
only when they are one object.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; it follows two
decisions of the revival.
By the first, of 6~November 2026, the values of the arbitrary-precision integer
and rational types are value objects: \library\ declare the arbitrary-precision
integer as a value object, and the sentence's own list called integers value
objects and arbitrary-precision numbers reference objects, so the text
disagreed with itself and with the library; the library's declaration is the
deliberate word.
By the second, of 6 and 7~November 2026, strictly equivalent means the rule of
\secref{equivalence} on both implementations, with no special case for any type,
and strings are reference objects: \library\ declare every kind of string as an
object without the \KWD{value} modifier, so two strings are strictly equivalent
only when they are one object, and their text equality is their own \EXP{=}.
The Working Draft of February 2011 named no kind for strings, and the
team's implementations compared two flat strings by their text and two ropes
by identity.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md}, section~2.4, and
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/string-equivalence-2026-11-06.md} in the
revival's repository.
\item[Effect] Both implementations answer \EXP{\sequiv} by the rule, and both
read the \KWD{value} modifier.
\Library\ declare the rational type's object and the two numeral objects of the
interpreter as value objects.
The departures:
the interpreter gives a floating-point numeral bound to a variable of type
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} the type of the numeral object, so it is not strictly
equivalent to a computed \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} value of the same bits;
an integer numeral is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} value in the interpreter, by its magnitude, and a numeral
object to the compiled type checker, so a numeral
compared with a typed value can answer differently on the two paths;
the compiled path's own library, used until the one library replaces it,
answers \EXP{\sequiv} on values of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64},
\EXP{\mathbb{R}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, on strings and on booleans by
\EXP{=} before it
reaches the rule, so there two equal strings built apart are strictly
equivalent and \EXP{0.0} is strictly equivalent to \EXP{-0.0} (row~908 of the
revival's gap ledger);
and \library\ declare \EXP{=} on pairs and triples only, so two tuples of four

51:- P-54 **`QQ`'s `ceiling` and `truncate` keep `ZZ`, their declared result type, and raise an error at +∞, −∞ and 0/0.** The specification's paragraph on these methods said that they return the argument itself at those three values (`Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex`, "Rational Numbers"). That paragraph is revised. `floor`, `round` and the brackets ⌊x⌋ and ⌈x⌉ are built on `ceiling` and `truncate`, so they raise too. Why: the declared integer result and other languages win over the paragraph: Python's `math.floor(inf)`, for one, raises. The library raises `DivisionByZero`, as the revised paragraph says. After the switch-over, `QQ` follows the float ruling (P-68, on rounding the float types): `floor` and `ceiling` return `QQ` and pass the infinities through, and the brackets, `round` and `truncate` give `ZZ` (row 795).
96:- P-159 **A float compared with a NaN answers: `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` give `false`, and `CMP` gives `Unordered`, on both paths.** On `RR64` and `RR32` the four ordering operators answer `false` when either side is a NaN, and `CMP` answers `Unordered`, as the team built them. `FloatingComparisonError` stays declared in both libraries, and nothing raises it. The specification's overview of operators said that this comparison threw that error, and the sentence before it that a rational comparison at 1/0 or 0/0 threw `RationalComparisonError` (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:283-288`). Both sentences are revised, in the form of Appendix I, to the rationals chapter's reading: 0/0 compares `false` "for compatibility with floating-point arithmetic", and the infinities are ordered (F-319). Row 672 closed with that edit. Why: a NaN test in software would slow the comparison against the hardware's own; measured, it is noise on today's boxed compiled path and costs 15 to 20 percent a comparison on unboxed doubles in Java, and whether it stops vectorisation is open (`perf-probes/nan-check-cost/REPORT.md`). The team built `false` and `Unordered` everywhere and never raised the error, and Java, Swift, Python's floats, Julia and Haskell all answer `false`.
102:- P-172 **A numeral with a radix point has a type of its own, `FloatLiteral`, which holds the numeral's exact value: `QQ` converts from it exactly, and `RR64` and `RR32` with one rounding.** `FloatLiteral` stands beside the number types, as the compiler's prelude declares it (`trait FloatLiteral excludes {RR32, RR64}`, `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:996`), in place of the interpreter library's `value object FloatLiteral extends RR64` (`FortressBuiltin.fsi:44`). So `3.125` converts to the `QQ` value `3125/1000`, `q: QQ = 0.5` binds and `1/2 = 0.5` is `true`; into `RR64` or `RR32` a numeral rounds once, to the type's nearest value, on both paths (row 862: the compiled path rounds two or three times). `QQ`, `RR64` and `RR32` each declare the pair of `=` that goes with each coercion (P-165). Where nothing fixes a type, as at a parameter of type `Any` or a static argument that only the numeral fixes, the numeral stays an exact `FloatLiteral`: `Cell(0.5)` is a `Cell[\FloatLiteral\]` on both paths. Walk converts a `FloatLiteral` where `RR64` or `RR32` is declared, at a binding, a parameter and a field, so `y: RR64 = 0.5` is `SEQV` a computed `0.25 + 0.25`; it prints a bare numeral as written, as the team's `tests/NumberPrintTest.fss:16` asserts. The specification's literals chapter and the coercions of `basic-lib/numbers.tex:43` follow, with an Appendix I entry, in the revision form (P-96). Not decided here: `round` of a numeral within half an ulp of a tie, which rounds the double, not the rational (row 360), and two bare numerals of one value, such as `2.5` and `2.50`, which are `SEQV` but print as written. No line of microGPT changes, and its numerals keep their bits. Why: the Working Draft keeps a numeral unconverted, since "converting it immediately to a floating-point number may lose precision", gives 3.125 "the rational value 3125/1000", has the library coerce a compound numeral to the rationals, and converts a static rational expression into a float with "at most one floating-point rounding error" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-173`); the curator reads it so: nothing is lost in `QQ`, and a float of fixed size takes one rounding. The prelude declares `FloatLiteral` apart, with the coercions into `RR64` and `RR32` (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:932`, `:993`), and P-76 took that design for integer numerals.

Load can lengthen a stage more than twofold: climb batch 16's merged code took 217 s for the distance stage at its gate, at a load average of 3.3, and nearly the same code took 574 s at 4.6 to 5.3. \section{Static Expressions}
\seclabel{static-expr}

\note{Of the static expressions in a size, the interpreter computes a sum, a
difference, a product and a power exactly, and refuses a power at a negative
exponent; the compiled type checker computes each operation on numerals,
refusing as out of range a power it does not compute, and compares other size
expressions by their written form (\chapref{types}); the compiled path
computes a size when it names a class. The compiled type checker does not
infer a \KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim} or \KWD{unit} static argument.}

\emph{Static expressions} denote \emph{static values}.  Conceptually,
a static expression is not evaluated while a program is running, and
thus its evaluation
cannot complete abruptly.  Given instantiations of all static
parameters (described in \chapref{trait-parameters}) in scope of a
static expression, the value of the static expression can be
determined statically.  Static expressions which use a restricted subset of operations can occur as
\emph{static arguments} which instantiate static parameters and
\KWD{where}-clause constraints (described in \secref{where-clauses}).
We define the set of static
expressions by first defining the types of static expressions, and
distinguishing static values from the closely related literal values.
We then describe the expressions that evaluate to the various kinds of
static values.


\subsection{Types of Static Expressions}

There are three groups of traits that describe literals
and static expressions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The \emph{literal} traits, which describe boolean,
  character, string, and numerals.  For example, the literal \VAR{true} has
  trait \EXP{\TYP{BooleanLiteral}\llbracket\VAR{true}\rrbracket} and a
  character literal has trait \TYP{Character}.
See \secref{literals} for a discussion of Fortress literals.

\item The \emph{constant} traits, which describe values denoted by
expressions composed from literals and operators (described in
\secref{constant-values});
the type of a constant expression encodes the value of the expression.
For example, the type of a constant expression \EXP{3+5},
%IntegerConstant[\false, 3+5\]
\EXP{\TYP{IntegerConstant}\llbracket\VAR{false}, 3+5\rrbracket},
encodes the value of the expression; the operator \EXP{+} is
used in the static arguments.  When an operator is not supported in static
arguments, \library\ can still encode the value of the expression by
providing a specific constant trait such as
\EXP{\TYP{RationalValueTimesPi}\llbracket\VAR{false},1,1\rrbracket}
(described in \secref{pi}).



\item The \emph{static} traits, which describe values denoted by
expressions composed from literals, operators (described in
\secref{constant-values}), and \KWD{bool}, \KWD{nat},
and \KWD{int} parameters; here the type
does not encode the value of the expression, but the value of the
expression can nevertheless be known statically if specific
values are specified for the static parameters.  Also, in situations

For example, \EXP{\mathtt{deadc}_{16} \| \mathtt{0de}_{16}} yields \EXP{\mathtt{deadc0de}_{16}}.

Every literal trait extends an appropriate constant trait, and every
constant trait extends an appropriate static trait.  So every
literal is also a constant expression, and every constant expression
is a static expression.

The specification calls it "logical equivalence" on booleans (basic-lib/booleans.tex:256-261), but today a program writes a <-> b for that. The skill's sentence now says so, and the next change on this page shows it.

##### AR12. 2026-11-08T07:02:10.759Z · line 2360 · reply on thread `4e0493d3` (COORDINATOR)

> The skill already has all three spellings, and it tells the two look-alike symbols apart. This item, change 39, still shows the text as it landed with climb batch 27. The fix is change 51, further down this page (commits e9f828f3 and 4ccaeaaf).
> 
> The rule in revival-changes.md, "Traits and objects", now reads:
> 
> "Strict equivalence is the operator ≣ (STRICTLY EQUIVALENT TO), written SEQV or === in ASCII. The operator ≡ (IDENTICAL TO, EQV or EQUIV) is a different one: logical equivalence on booleans. The interpreter's library declares it for no type, and walk stops on it (row 184): write a <-> b."
> 
> So the three ways to write strict equivalence are:
> - ≣, the Unicode symbol, U+2263, with four bars;
> - SEQV, the operator's name in capitals;
> - ===, the ASCII spelling.
> 
> The look-alike is ≡, U+2261, with three bars. It is spelled EQV or EQUIV, and it is a different operator.
> 
> Specification/appendices/operators.tex:418-419 gives both.

## E. The coordinator's three asks and his answers

### E1. Ask 1 (string literals) · COORDINATOR · 2026-11-08T11:58:34.110Z · line 3191

~~~~
**Ask 1 of 7, string literals: should two string literals with the same text be one object, so that `"ab" SEQV "ab"` is true?**

Context:
- `SEQV` (`≣`, `===`) asks whether two values are one value. By your decision P-168, a string is a reference object: two strings are `SEQV` only if they are one object, and text equality is `=`.
- Today, on both paths, each evaluation of a string literal makes a new object. So `"ab" SEQV "ab"` is false, and so is `f() SEQV f()` for `f(): String = "ab"`. `"ab" = "ab"` is true. In Java, `"ab" == "ab"` is true, because Java interns literals: it keeps one object per text.
- **The specification** doesn't say whether a literal is one object. "Literals are values; they do not require evaluation" (`literals.tex:25-26`) leans that way.
- **The team's later word** is the 2012 restart: "All literals represent value objects; therefore their values do not have object identity" (`literals.tick:29`). P-25 gives the restart's full weight only to its Types chapter.
- **The team's code:** walk (2008) and the compiler prelude (2010) both compared strings by text. Its test `seqv.fss:22` asserts `"cat" === "cat"`. P-168 accepted that this test fails at the switch-over.
- **Peers, as context:** Java, C#, Scala and Kotlin intern literals. Swift, Julia and Haskell give strings no identity at all.
- The switch-over doesn't need the answer. microGPT doesn't use `SEQV`, so nothing changes for it.

Options:
1. **Intern string literals and keep P-168.** Literals with the same text are one object on both paths. A string built at run time stays a separate object.
   - Walk: about 3 lines in the evaluator, a table from text to string object.
   - Compiled: an intern table at each literal site, about 15 lines, which matches walk exactly.
   - The worker tried walk's change, without building: none of the 51 walk tests it ran changed, and `seqv.fss:22` passes again.
   - The specification gains one sentence, "a string literal denotes one object", with an Appendix I entry.
   - Cost: one small rung.

   1b. Also fold `"foo" || "bar"` into one literal at compile time, as `constant.tex:81-85` says. Then `("foo" || "bar") SEQV "foobar"` is true, as with Java's constant expressions. About half a rung more.
2. **Make strings value objects, compared by text.** A computed `"ab"` is then `SEQV` a literal `"ab"` too.
   - This reverses P-168's ruling on strings.
   - The string lines of the two strict-equivalence tests flip.
   - Cost: one rung.
3. **Keep today's behaviour.** Record it as a contested ledger row, and `seqv.fss:22` fails at the switch-over, as you accepted.

How they weigh:
- Option 1 keeps your rule and removes the cost you accepted with it. It agrees with every team source that speaks about literals. Computed strings stay reference objects.
- Option 2 follows the restart's wording and the team's code more closely, but it undoes a decision you made on the specification's rule.
- Option 3 costs nothing now and keeps the surprise you named.
- Strings showing up as `FlatString` in generics (`Cell("s")` is a `Cell[\FlatString\]`) is a separate fix. It comes with the row 364 ask.

The argument is in section 6.1: https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/reviews/literals-2026-11-08.md

My recommendation is 1 in climb batch 29, and 1b if you also want Java's constant rule.

component NumberPrintTest
export Executable

run() = do
  assert("" 3.1415926535897932384000000000001, "3.1415926535897932384000000000001")
  assert("" 43, "43")
  assert("" 12367125, "12367125")

  zep = big(1)
  println (-zep)
  foo = 78236427658757685
  bar = -foo
  println foo
  println bar
  yelp(x: Number) =
    typecase x of
      IntLiteral => println "IntLiteral"
      BigNum => println "BigNum"
      ZZ32 => println "ZZ32"
      ZZ64 => println "ZZ64"
      NN32 => println "NN32"
      UnsignedLong => println "UnsignedLong"
      NN64 => println "NN64"
      ZZ => println "ZZ"
    end
  yelp foo

The arrays' 7, of `PrimitiveArray`, `PrimImmutableArray` and `PrimImmutableRR64Array`: the compiled half by P-164's device, a store trait in `FortressLibrary` whose bindings name helpers of a new `nativeHelpers/arrayOps` over a compiled class that holds the elements; `PrimitiveArray` and `PrimImmutableArray` leave the native component and hold the store in a field, and walk's native object below the trait holds an `AtomicArray`; `PrimImmutableRR64Array`'s two are on a compiled `double[]` class that no factory chooses until array decision A (P-84, P-85; F-333). The compiled store is an `Object[]`, and the compiled transaction tracks its reads and writes by the array and the index (`TXReadSlot`, `TXWriteSlot`): P-84 stores every number type's array unboxed, so a compiled `atomic` write into any array needs that keying, and an array of objects keeps one box an element, not two. Threads, `abort` and the task trace, 6: helpers in a `nativeHelpers` class over the compiled runtime, as the team's `nativeHelpers/runtime.java` is (F-335); `Thread`'s `val`, `wait`, `ready` and `stop` raise until the code generator compiles `spawn` (row 82). The numerals, 32: `IntLiteral`'s 8 conversions and comparisons are Fortress text over its `asZZ` (F-331);

POSITIONS.md:40
- P-43 **The exclusion rule stays, and the number tower is flat (route A).** The compiled checker keeps the multiple instantiation exclusion rule. So the library's numbers are flat, as the team (Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen) flattened the compiler prelude in 2009 and 2010. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`, each with its own algebra, and `Number` has no catch-all operators. Why: the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way, and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule. He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen. F-46 prices a return to route C.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The standard and the sources

POSITIONS.md:24
- P-26 **The team's later decision wins over its earlier one, in a text or in code, where the team made it the language's rule.** P-7 names the texts, from the Working Draft to the POPL 2019 paper. Code counts as a decision where the team built it alike for all its types, or stated its rule in a commit message, a comment or the checker. Code that its author called a stub, and code that works around a limit of the JVM or of the checker, serve only the implementation. The decision that they depart from stands. "Later" is the date of the team's work on the point at issue. The revival revises `Specification/` to follow a later decision. The one library follows it too, in place of the team's earlier code, such as the interpreter's library. Where two later decisions conflict, the goal decides (P-8). The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. Why: the Working Draft's early text was a wish. The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run. So they learned what is feasible. They sought performance, and specialization was a must. Their later decisions include the exclusion rule, specialization and the number types of the compiler's prelude, siblings from 2009 to 2012 (P-43). The revival knows less than they did, so it does not second-guess them.

POSITIONS.md:23
- P-25 **`Specification/` stays the standard, and the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart is cited beside it.** The restart is a new specification that the team began in 2012 and left unfinished (F-166). Where its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, a worker cites it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word. On the rules that the revival revises, such as the exclusion rule, the chapter is the designers' latest intent, which the goal is to finish, and `Specification/` is revised to follow it. Three of the chapter's passages bear on the specification; P-97 holds how the revision uses the first two. It names the exclusion rule "instantiation exclusion" and gives it in two parts: which instantiations of a generic exclude each other (`types.tick:355-360`), and, in its note, a rule on trait declarations (`:361-376`). The revised `Specification/` takes that form: the first part in its chapter on types, the second in its chapter on traits. # Literals in revived Fortress: one picture

## The shape the curator saw

Three surprises, each on strict equivalence, `SEQV` (also `===` or `≣`), which asks "one value?", not "same text?":

```
"ab" SEQV "ab"            (* false on both paths today *)
y: RR64 = 0.5
x: RR64 = 0.25 + 0.25
y SEQV x                  (* false under walk today *)
z: ZZ32 = 3
3 SEQV z                  (* true under walk, false compiled *)
```

They have one cause. In each, a path lets its own storage of a literal decide what the program sees:
- Strings: each evaluation of a literal makes a new object, on both paths.
- Floats: the interpreter's library declares its numeral type below `RR64`, so a typed `RR64` place converts nothing.
- Integers: walk stores a numeral as its internal class `Int` and builds generics at it. So `Cell(3)` is a `Cell[\Int\]`, a type apart from `Cell[\ZZ32\]`.

This is what the curator named "the representation of literals" and "the interpreter's internals leaking out to user land". The cure is one rule that both paths follow.

## The rule, for every kind of literal

1. **A literal names one value, fixed by its text.** Every evaluation gives that value.
2. **Its type holds that value exactly.** A string literal is a `String`: one type holds every text. No one number type holds every numeral: `ZZ32` misses `3000000000`, and `RR64` misses `0.1`. So a numeral has a type of its own that holds its exact value: `IntLiteral` for an integer numeral (P-76), `FloatLiteral` for a numeral with a radix point (P-172).
3. **It converts once, where a type is fixed**, by the library's declared conversions. Where nothing fixes a type, it keeps its own type.
4. **`SEQV` and `=` then follow the value.** Two values of different types are never `SEQV`. Numbers compare by type and value. A string is `SEQV` only to the same object (P-168). `=` is each type's own equality.
5. **An expression of literals alone is a literal.** The team's draft folds `"foo" || "bar"` into `"foobar"`, and computes numeral arithmetic exactly, with "at most one floating-point rounding error".

## Where the kinds differ by nature

- A number is a value object: it has no identity. A string is a reference object: it has one (P-168). Rule 1 joins them: one literal text is one object (P-171).
- A string converts into no other type; a numeral converts into several. So strings are not the odd one: their own type happens to be a library type. Character and boolean literals are the same.

## Where a literal converts

A place fixes a type when it declares one: a typed binding or assignment, a parameter, a field, a return type, or a written static argument, as `Cell[\ZZ32\](3)`.

A place fixes no type where the declared type is `Any`, or where only the literal fixes a static argument. So `Cell(3)` is a `Cell[\IntLiteral\]`. The team's text: coercion occurs only where the parameter type "is exactly the type" converted to.

Where a numeral's conversions tie, it reads as `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by size. This is the specification's rule for integer numerals. It has no float half yet.

On each path:
- Compiled today: the checker converts at typed places. At `Any` a numeral keeps its type.
- Walk today: it has no static types. It converts at run time, by the value (P-59). Its float numeral is already an `RR64`, and its integer numeral a `ZZ32`, from the start.
- After the switch-over: the compiled path reads the interpreter's library (P-37). Walk then runs the checker and uses its conversions (P-12).

## `SEQV` and `=` once both decisions are built

Strings (P-171):
```
b = "b"
"ab" SEQV "ab"            (* true: one object *)
"ab" SEQV ("a" || "b")    (* true: folded *)
"ab" SEQV ("a" || b)      (* false: built at run time *)
"ab" = ("a" || b)         (* true: same text *)
```

Floats (P-172):
```
y SEQV x                  (* true: y converted where declared *)
0.5 SEQV x                (* false: FloatLiteral, RR64 *)
0.5 = x                   (* true *)
q: QQ = 0.5               (* binds, exactly 1/2 *)
```

Integers (the decision that gives an integer numeral its own type, P-76, as the compiled path does it):
```
3 SEQV 3                  (* true *)
3 SEQV z                  (* false: IntLiteral, ZZ32 *)
3 = z                     (* true *)
```

## What the team's sources say

They agree on the shape:
- A literal denotes one fixed value: the Working Draft and the 2012 restart.
- A string literal is a `String` in every source.
- A numeral has its own type and the library converts it: the Working Draft and the compiler's prelude, the team's later word (P-26).

The team left the shape uneven in four places:
- It held three numeral designs. Draft and prelude: own type, converted. The interpreter's library: a type below a default, `FloatLiteral extends RR64`, held "until coercion is implemented". The restart: a library type at the parse, `QQ` or `NN`.
- In the prelude, `IntLiteral` is a `Number` and `FloatLiteral` is not. The prelude has no `QQ`.
- No source says whether a string literal is one object.
- The draft folds strings and numerals. The team built only the integer fold, compiled.

The papers say nothing on literals.

## What is not yet uniform

- **Float ties.** `1.0 s`, for `s: ZZ32`, fits both `QQ`'s and `RR64`'s product by conversion. Only a float half of the tie rule, `RR64`, picks one. By reading, microGPT needs it.
- **Float folding.** Without rule 5, `(0.25 + 0.25) SEQV 0.5` is false.
- **Printing and rounding.** `2.5` and `2.50` are `SEQV` but print differently, and `round` rounds the double. Rule 1 says: print and round the exact value. P-172 left both open.
- **Walk's types.** Walk builds generics at `Int` and `FlatString`. The curator asked for this walk defect to be fixed now.
- **Walk's integer numeral** stays a `ZZ32` until walk runs the checker, so `3 SEQV z` stays true there.

**The one fork.** The rule answers every place above but one: a place that fixes no type. Does a numeral keep its own type there, or take a default, as in Swift? The curator answered for floats: it keeps its type (P-172). The rule asks the same for integers, which is P-76 as it stands, so `3 SEQV z` is false. A default for integers alone splits the two numeral kinds. A default for both reverses that clause of P-172, and no team source asks for it.

## The plan

Seven rungs. Sizes by reading. Tests run on both paths unless marked.
1. **One object per string literal** (P-171). Walk interns each literal; both paths compare the carried Java strings by `==`; a shared phase folds two literals joined by `||`. About 3 and 4 lines; the fold is not sized. Asserts the four string lines above.
2. **`FloatLiteral` apart, in the library and the checker** (P-172). `QQ`, `RR64` and `RR32` convert from it, with their `=`; the tie rule gains `RR64`; compiled numerals round once. About 15 to 30 library lines; the rest not sized. Asserts `q: QQ = 0.5`, `1/2 = 0.5`, `Cell(0.5)` a `Cell[\FloatLiteral\]`, `1.0 s` an `RR64`.
3. **Walk converts a `FloatLiteral` at each typed place**, and breaks float ties. About 20 lines. Asserts `y SEQV x`, under walk.
4. **Walk shows only language types.** Its inference reads `Int` as `ZZ32` and its string objects as `String`; its messages print the traits. 40 to 50 lines for numbers; strings and messages not sized. Asserts `Just(z) = Just[\ZZ32\](z)` and that `Cell("s")` takes a declaration over `Cell[\String\]`, under walk.
5. **A float numeral prints and rounds by its value.** Not sized. Asserts `"" 2.50 = "2.5"`; the team's print test keeps passing. Needs the curator's word.
6. **Numeral expressions fold exactly**, in a shared phase. Not sized. Asserts `(0.25 + 0.25) SEQV 0.5`. Needs the curator's word.
7. **Walk's integer numeral becomes an `IntLiteral`**, with P-12. Asserts `3 SEQV z` false under walk. It can come earlier on rung 3's conversion; a probe of that measured 24 passing tests failing (F-74).

## The switch-over and microGPT

- The distance to the switch-over is 0 errors and the checker count 0 at the last gate (F-53). Only rung 2 changes what the checker reads, so both stages measure it.
- The switch-over needs rung 2 first. Without it, the compiled path takes `FloatLiteral` below `RR64`, and `y SEQV x` turns false there.
- No line of microGPT changes if rung 2 has the float tie rule. Without it, by reading, `1 - beta1`, `beta1^t` and `1.0 s` (flat program lines 77 to 82) tie. Neither program uses `SEQV`.
EOF

# Literals in revived Fortress: one picture

## The shape the curator saw

Strict equivalence, `SEQV` (also `===` or `≣`), asks "one value?", not "same text?". Three cases surprised him:

```
"ab" SEQV "ab"            (* false on both paths *)
y: RR64 = 0.5
x: RR64 = 0.25 + 0.25
y SEQV x                  (* false under walk *)
z: ZZ32 = 3
3 SEQV z                  (* true under walk, false compiled *)
```

One cause: each path lets its own storage of a literal decide what a program sees.
- Strings: each evaluation makes a new object, on both paths.
- Floats: walk's library puts its numeral type below `RR64`, so a typed place converts nothing.
- Integers: walk stores a numeral as its class `Int`, so `Cell(3)` is a `Cell[\Int\]`, apart from `Cell[\ZZ32\]`.

He named it "the representation of literals" and "internals leaking out to user land". The cure is one rule on both paths.

## The rule, for every kind of literal

1. **A literal names one value, fixed by its text.** Every evaluation gives that value.
2. **Its type holds that value exactly.** `String` holds every text. No number type holds every numeral (`ZZ32` misses `3000000000`, `RR64` misses `0.1`), so a numeral has a type of its own: `IntLiteral` (P-76), or `FloatLiteral` with a radix point (P-172).
3. **It converts once, where a type is fixed**, by the library's conversions. Elsewhere it keeps its own type.
4. **`SEQV` and `=` follow the value** (P-168). Values of two types are never `SEQV`. Numbers compare by value; a string by being the same object. `=` is each type's own equality.
5. **An expression of literals alone is a literal.** The team's Working Draft of 2011 folds `"foo" || "bar"`, and computes numeral arithmetic exactly, with "at most one floating-point rounding error".

## Where the kinds differ by nature

- A number is a value object, with no identity. A string is a reference object, with one (P-168). Rule 1 joins them: one literal text is one object (P-171).
- A string converts into no other type; a numeral into several. Strings are not the odd one: their own type is a library type.

## Where a literal converts

A place fixes a type when it declares one: a typed binding or assignment, a parameter, a field, a return type, a written static argument.

A parameter of type `Any` fixes none, nor does a static argument that only the literal fixes: `Cell(3)` is a `Cell[\IntLiteral\]`. The team's text: coercion occurs only where the parameter type "is exactly the type" converted to.

Where an integer numeral's conversions tie, it reads as `ZZ32`, or wider by size. No float half exists yet.

- Compiled today: the checker converts at typed places.
- Walk today: no static types; it converts by the run-time value (P-59). Its numerals are an `RR64` subtype and a `ZZ32` from the start.
- After the switch-over: one library (P-37); walk runs the checker and uses its conversions (P-12).

## `SEQV` and `=` once both decisions are built

Strings (P-171):
```
b = "b"
"ab" SEQV ("a" || "b")    (* true: folded *)
"ab" SEQV ("a" || b)      (* false: built at run time *)
"ab" = ("a" || b)         (* true: same text *)
```

Floats (P-172):
```
y SEQV x                  (* true *)
0.5 SEQV x                (* false: FloatLiteral, RR64 *)
0.5 = x                   (* true *)
```

Integers (P-76), as compiled today:
```
3 SEQV z                  (* false: IntLiteral, ZZ32 *)
3 = z                     (* true *)
```

## What the team's sources say

They agree: a literal denotes one fixed value (the Working Draft, the 2012 restart); a string literal is a `String`; a numeral has its own type, converted by the library (the draft and the compiler's library, the team's later word, P-26).

Uneven in four places:
- Three numeral designs: own type, converted (draft, compiler); a type below a default, `FloatLiteral extends RR64` (interpreter's library); `QQ` or `NN` (restart).
- The compiler's `IntLiteral` is a `Number`, its `FloatLiteral` not, and it has no `QQ`.
- No source says whether a string literal is one object.
- The draft folds strings and numerals; the team built only the integer fold, compiled.

The papers are silent.

## What is not yet uniform

- **Float ties.** `1.0 s`, for `s: ZZ32`, fits `QQ`'s and `RR64`'s product by conversion. A float tie rule, `RR64`, picks one.
- **Float folds.** Without rule 5, `(0.25 + 0.25) SEQV 0.5` is false.
- **Printing and rounding.** `2.5` and `2.50` are `SEQV` but print apart; `round` rounds the double. Rule 1: use the exact value. The float decision left both open.
- **Walk's types.** Walk builds generics at `Int` and `FlatString`. He asked for a fix now.
- **Walk's integer numeral** stays a `ZZ32` until walk runs the checker.

**The one fork.** The rule answers each place but one: a place that fixes no type. Does a numeral keep its own type there, or take a default, as in Swift? He answered for floats: it keeps it (P-172). The rule asks the same for integers, as the integer decision says: `3 SEQV z` is false. A default for integers alone splits the numeral kinds; for both, it reverses a clause of the float decision, and no team source asks for it.

## The plan

Seven rungs, sized by reading. Tests run on both paths unless marked.
1. **One object per string literal** (P-171): walk interns; both paths compare the carried Java strings by `==`; a shared phase folds `||` of two literals. About 3 and 4 lines; fold not sized. Asserts the string lines above.
2. **`FloatLiteral` apart** (P-172): `QQ`, `RR64`, `RR32` convert from it, with their `=`; ties read `RR64`; compiled numerals round once. 15 to 30 library lines; the rest not sized. Asserts `q: QQ = 0.5`, `1/2 = 0.5`, `Cell(0.5)` a `Cell[\FloatLiteral\]`, `1.0 s` an `RR64`.

content.content:
# Literals in revived Fortress: one picture

## The shape the curator saw

Strict equivalence, `SEQV` (also `===` or `≣`), asks "one value?", not "same text?". Three cases surprised him:

```
"ab" SEQV "ab"            (* false on both paths *)
y: RR64 = 0.5
x: RR64 = 0.25 + 0.25
y SEQV x                  (* false under walk *)
z: ZZ32 = 3
3 SEQV z                  (* walk true, compiled false *)
```

One cause: each path lets its storage of a literal decide what a program sees.
- Strings: each evaluation makes a new object, on both paths.
- Floats: the interpreter's library puts its numeral type below `RR64`; a typed place converts nothing.
- Integers: walk stores `3` as its class `Int`; `Cell(3)` is a `Cell[\Int\]`, apart from `Cell[\ZZ32\]`.

He named it "the representation of literals" and "the interpreter's internals leaking out to user land". The fix: one rule on both paths.

## The rule, for every kind of literal

1. **A literal names one value, fixed by its text.** Each evaluation gives that value.
2. **Its type holds that value exactly.** `String` holds every text. No number type holds every numeral (`ZZ32` misses `3000000000`, `RR64` misses `0.1`), so a numeral has its own type: `IntLiteral` (P-76), or `FloatLiteral` with a radix point (P-172).
3. **It converts once, where a type is fixed**, by the library's conversions. Elsewhere it keeps its own type.
4. **`SEQV` and `=` follow the value** (P-168). Values of two types are never `SEQV`. Numbers compare by value; a string by being the same object. `=` is each type's own equality.
5. **An expression of literals alone is a literal.** The team's Working Draft of 2011 folds `"foo" || "bar"` and computes numeral arithmetic exactly: "at most one floating-point rounding error".

## Where the kinds differ by nature

- A number is a value object, with no identity; a string a reference object, with one (P-168). Rule 1 serves both: one literal text is one object (P-171).
- A string converts into no other type; a numeral into several. Strings are not the odd one: their own type is a library type.

## Where a literal converts

A place fixes a type when it declares one: a typed binding or assignment, a parameter, a field, a return type, a written static argument.

A parameter of type `Any` fixes none, nor does a static argument that only the literal fixes: `Cell(3)` is a `Cell[\IntLiteral\]`. The coercion chapter agrees.

Where an integer numeral's conversions tie, it reads as `ZZ32`, or wider by size; no float rule exists.

- Compiled today: the checker converts at typed places.
- Walk today: no static types; it converts by the run-time value (P-59). Its float numeral is below `RR64`; its integer numeral is a `ZZ32`.
- After the switch-over: one library (P-37); walk runs the checker and uses its conversions (P-12).

## `SEQV` and `=` after the two decisions

Strings (P-171):
```
b = "b"
"ab" SEQV ("a" || "b")    (* true: folded *)
"ab" SEQV ("a" || b)      (* false: built at run time *)
"ab" = ("a" || b)         (* true *)
```

Floats (P-172):
```
y SEQV x                  (* true *)
0.5 SEQV x                (* false: FloatLiteral, RR64 *)
0.5 = x                   (* true *)
```

Integers (P-76), compiled today:
```
3 SEQV z                  (* false: IntLiteral, ZZ32 *)
3 = z                     (* true *)
```

## The team's sources

They agree: a literal denotes one fixed value (the Working Draft, the 2012 restart); a string literal is a `String`; a numeral has its own type, converted by the library (the draft and the compiler's library, the later word, P-26).

Uneven in four places:
- Three numeral designs: own type, converted (draft, compiler); below a default, `FloatLiteral extends RR64` (interpreter's library); `QQ` or `NN` (restart).
- The compiler's `IntLiteral` is a `Number`, its `FloatLiteral` not; it has no `QQ`.
- No source says whether a string literal is one object.
- The draft folds strings and numerals; the team built only the integer fold, on the compiled path.

The papers say nothing.

## What is not yet uniform

- **Float ties.** `1.0 s`, for `s: ZZ32`, fits `QQ`'s and `RR64`'s product by conversion; a float tie rule, `RR64`, picks one.
- **Float folds.** Without rule 5, `(0.25 + 0.25) SEQV 0.5` is false.
- **Printing and rounding.** `2.5` and `2.50` are `SEQV` but print apart; `round` rounds the double. The float decision left both open; rule 1 says: the exact value.
- **Walk's types.** Walk builds generics at `Int` and `FlatString`; he asked for a fix now.
- **Walk's integer numeral** is a `ZZ32` until walk runs the checker.

**The one fork** is a place that fixes no type. Does a numeral keep its own type there, or take a default, as in Swift? He took "keeps it" for floats (P-172). The rule asks the same for integers, as the integer decision says: `3 SEQV z` is false. His words of 08:03 lean to a default; his rule of 12:36 named only typed places. A default for integers alone splits the numeral kinds; for both, it reverses a clause of the float decision. No team source asks for it.

## The plan

Seven rungs, sized by reading; tests on both paths unless marked.
1. **One object per string literal** (P-171): walk interns; both paths compare the carried Java strings by `==`; a shared phase folds `||` of two literals. About 3 and 4 lines; fold not sized. Asserts the string lines.
2. **`FloatLiteral` apart** (P-172): `QQ`, `RR64`, `RR32` convert from it, with their `=`; ties read `RR64`; compiled numerals round once. 15 to 30 library lines; the rest not sized. Asserts `q: QQ = 0.5`, `1/2 = 0.5`, `Cell(0.5)` a `Cell[\FloatLiteral\]`, `1.0 s` an `RR64`.
